h: פּוּרִים, מַאֲמָר ה׳ Purim — Maamar Hei

p: The kelipah of Amalek and Haman
is brazenness and defiance toward Heaven,
and it is like the kelipah of Bilam:
for even though he was told,
לֹא תָאוֹר אֶת הָעָם וְגוֹ׳ [בְּמִדְבַּר כב, יב]
do not curse the people," etc. (Bamidbar 22:12),
they stood in brazenness toward Heaven
for Hashem Yisbarach created in holiness
the matter of prevailing over Heaven
"Sing to the One Who is prevailed upon
is prevailed upon and rejoices," etc.
And in the manner of what they said
מַאי עָבֵיד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וְכוּ׳
"What did HaKadosh Baruch Hu do?" etc.
'My children have prevailed over Me,'" etc.
that this itself is the will of Hashem Yisbarach,
that we be bold-faced to prevail over Him
about Levi, who spoke harsh words
and said, "You have ascended and sat on high," etc.;
and although he was punished for this
the brazenness and defiance toward Above,
but "his end is to perish forever,"
He has established His throne for judgment."

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkas HaTzaddik 46 — “‘Audacity is kingship without a crown’ … they derived it from Bilam, for Bilam gazed unto the footsteps of Mashiach and therefore knew this secret.” Rav Tzadok there explains why Bilam's audacity worked at all: it imitates a holy audacity, Knesses Yisrael drawing near on its own initiative, which belongs to Israel in the time before Mashiach. This is the root of the “one opposite the other” drawn below.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 105a — “Rav Nachman said: Audacity is effective even toward Heaven. At first it is written, 'Do not go with them,' but afterward it is written, 'Rise, go with them.' Rav Sheshes said: Audacity is kingship without a crown.” The first statement concerns Bilaam's persistence despite God's initial prohibition. Rav Tzadok contrasts this self-serving audacity with persistent intercession undertaken for Israel's good.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 119a — “Come and see: The Holy One, blessed be He, is unlike a mortal. A mortal is defeated and is distressed; the Holy One, blessed be He, is defeated and rejoices, as it is said: 'He said to destroy them, had not Moshe His chosen one stood in the breach before Him.'” The preceding teaching reads 'For the Conductor' as 'Sing to the One Whom they overcome and Who rejoices.' Its example is Moshe's successful intercession, establishing the holy form of 'victory' that the maamar contrasts with Amalek's opposition.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 59b — “Rabbi Yehoshua stood and said: 'It is not in Heaven.' Rabbi Yirmeyah explained: The Torah has already been given at Mount Sinai; we do not heed a heavenly voice, for You already wrote in the Torah at Sinai, 'Incline after the majority.' Rabbi Nasan met Eliyahu and asked: What was the Holy One, blessed be He, doing at that time? He replied: He smiled and said, 'My children have overcome Me; My children have overcome Me.'” The victory in this source is fidelity to the Torah's authorized human process of decision. It is the Divine will expressed through the children's response, the principle Rav Tzadok draws from the smile.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 49 — “In truth audacity does not apply to Israel at all, for Hashem desires and yearns for His children to prevail over Him … Among the nations, it is audacity against the true will of Hashem.” Rav Tzadok there gives the reason for the distinction drawn here: the tzaddik's forceful words are audacity only in appearance, while Amalek's and Bilam's succeed for a moment but have no true existence.

paragraphs.text: Taanis 25a — “Levi decreed a fast, but rain did not come. He said before Him: Master of the universe, You have ascended and sat on high, and You do not have mercy on Your children! Rain came, and Levi became lame. Rabbi Elazar said: A person must never cast words at Heaven, for a great man cast words at Heaven and became lame—and who was it? Levi.” The next discussion says both this incident and his demonstration of a difficult bow contributed to his injury. The story thus records the cost of his audacity together with the public benefit of the rain, both of which the maamar acknowledges.
